chapter_theme: The last twenty-four verses keep the four-gem form: each names four things under one verb or likeness (dies beneath, is death to, stays, grows, is a fault, is evil, is the light of). They range over learning and its absence, speech, the base and the worthy, women's conduct, kin and friendship, and close with chains from speech or the wife to understanding and release.

81.reading: Beauty and youth are said to die beneath poverty, lineage and family standing beneath want of learning, paddy beneath a tank that has no water, and a draught ox beneath a load beyond its strength.
81.nuance: Every item repeats கீழ்ச்சாம், 'dies beneath': each good thing is killed by what should be under it and is missing or too heavy. Lineage, in the Kural's terms a matter of birth, is set among things that need a support from below to live.

items.claim: beauty and youth die under poverty
lineage and family standing die under want of learning
paddy dies below a tank with no water in it
a draught ox dies under a load beyond its strength

82.reading: The good, those who walk the good path, and the base outcasts all have no town they call their own, while for those with something in hand every town is their town.
82.nuance: The refrain 'no town is their own' must mean opposite things: the good and the renouncer belong everywhere, the base are kept nowhere. The last line turns it again: for the man with means every town is his, so the belonging the first two earn by virtue the rich buy. கடைகள் (the lowest) is a word of contempt; whether it ranks people by birth or by conduct the verse does not say.

items.claim: the good have no single town of their own
those who go the good path have no town of their own
the worthless lowest have no town of their own
for those who have wealth in hand every town is their town

83.reading: For the unlearned man his own speech is death, for the soft-leaved plantain the fruit it bears is death, for those who do wrong dharma is death, and death too is the woman who lives wickedly in the house.
83.nuance: Each death comes from inside the one it kills: one's own words, one's own fruit, the dharma one breaks, one's own wife. The plantain, which dies after fruiting, is the image that holds the four together.

items.claim: his own words are death to the unlearned man
the fruit it bears is death to the plantain
dharma is death to those who do wrong
the wife who acts wickedly in the house is death

84.reading: Cultivated land gains its glory by water, a port town its greatness by the goods it trades, kings their glory by the land they rule, and a dancer his name by his dancing.
84.nuance: The king stands in a row with a field, a port and a dancer: each is great by the one thing it works on, so the king's glory is borrowed from the land he holds, not his own.

items.claim: cultivated land gains glory by water
a port town gains greatness by the goods it trades
kings gain glory by the land they rule
a dancer gains repute by his dance

85.reading: The verse names striving after one alone as the excellence of women's work, striving always after the good as the mind of the அந்தணர், striving for the land another rules as the excellence of kings' work, and leaving one's kin as striving after one's own ruin.
85.nuance: All four turn on ஊக்கல், striving, so the verse assigns each station its proper object of effort; the fourth breaks the pattern by naming a striving that ruins. ஒன்றூக்கல் for women is most likely single devotion to the husband. The அந்தணர் are given a mind rather than a rite, which leaves open whether the word names a birth-group or the virtuous.

items.claim: striving after one alone is the excellence of women's work
always striving after good is the mind of the அந்தணர்
striving for land another rules is the excellence of kings' work
abandoning one's kin is striving after ruin

norm.note: a period norm assigning women the single-minded devotion that is their proper work, beside the work proper to andhanar and kings

86.reading: The verse says one must not steal, since harsh things follow; must not cast off what is worthy; must not befriend the small; and must not take up enmity with anyone.
86.nuance: Four negatives in -ஆமை, each with வேண்டும். Only the first gives a reason (கடிய வருதலால்). யார்மாட்டும் can close the third line (befriend the small with no one) or open the fourth (take enmity with no one); the sense survives either way.

items.claim: not stealing is required, because cruel consequences come
not rejecting what is worthy is required
not befriending small-minded men is required
not taking up enmity is required

87.reading: The verse bids one increase friends by leading them to the good, stand proud against enemies when the time is known, eat sparingly wherever one is, and curb anger where it cannot take effect.
87.nuance: The four imperatives rhyme (பெருக்குக, தருக்குக, அருக்குக, சுருக்குக): two increase, two decrease. Friends grow by what one does for them, not by numbers. The anger rule is limited to where anger 'does not go', leaving open anger where it can prevail.

items.claim: friends are to be increased by leading them to the good
towards enemies one is to be proud, knowing the right time
food is to be kept scant wherever one is
anger where it cannot avail is to be curbed

88.reading: Sloth stays with those bound for ruin, cruelty stays with those who neglect care, good women stay within the bound of the shame they cherish, and the elephant stays at the post planted for it.
88.nuance: The verb நிற்கும், 'stays', joins a vice that settles in a person with a restraint that holds one. Good women's shame is set beside the elephant's post: the bound is chosen and cherished (பேணிய), yet it is a tether.

items.claim: sloth stays with those who are to perish
cruelty stays with those who neglect to care
good women stay within the bound of their cherished shame
the elephant stays at the post planted for it

norm.note: a period norm that good women keep within the limit set by நாண், compared to a tethered elephant

89.reading: The verse says learned அந்தணர் know the Veda, kings know victory joined with just rule, bowing is always the ornament of the worthy, and the last line sets a woman's humility apart, on one reading as her not being a torment.
89.nuance: Each station has its proper excellence and the worthy have humility for theirs. The last line (அஃதன்றி அணங்கல் வணங்கின்று பெண்) is obscure: it may say a woman's bowing is not being an அணங்கு to her husband, or that a bowing woman is no அணங்கு. அந்தண் புலவர் may also be 'gracious learned men'.

items.claim: learned அந்தணர் know the Veda
kings know victory together with just rule
bowing is at all times the ornament of the worthy
for a woman, beyond that, humility lies in not afflicting

norm.note: a period norm setting a separate humility for women beside the Veda of the andhanar and the victory of kings

90.reading: A woman of good character keeps to the way she was set in, one without a bond goes as she pleases though guarded, desire goes where it went though checked, and a killing, though hidden, rests on the killer.
90.nuance: The common claim is that inner nature outruns outward control: guarding, blocking and hiding all fail. Desire and murder are the general cases that make the point about women more than a point about women.

items.claim: a woman of good character keeps to the way set for her
a woman with no bond goes as she pleases even when guarded
desire goes on where it was going even when obstructed
a killing, though concealed, rests on the killer

norm.note: a period view of women's conduct as fixed by character, against which guarding them is useless

91.reading: Where hardness of eye grows strength grows, where the sweet looks of soft-spoken women grow kin grow, where the gentle eye of the worthy grows dharma grows, and where the hard eye of the base grows sin is great.
91.nuance: The same வன்கண் opens and closes the verse: in the first line it is daring that brings strength, in the last the hard eye of the base that brings sin. The eye is the measure throughout: hard, sweet, gentle, hard again.

items.claim: where hardness of eye grows, strength grows
where the sweet looks of women of milky speech grow, kin grow
where the gentle eye of the worthy grows, dharma grows
where the hard eye of the base grows, sin is great

92.reading: Not learning in youth, being liberal when one has no means, anger when one has no kin, and eating from the hand of those not one's own are each named a fault.
92.nuance: Every fault is a virtue or need out of its time or place: learning missed in its season, giving without the means for it, anger without kin to stand behind it, food taken from strangers. The last is about dependence, not purity.

items.claim: not learning in youth is a fault
liberality at a time without means is a fault
anger when one has no kin is a fault
eating from the hand of those not one's own is a fault

93.reading: Killing is evil in every place, letting one's children grow up unlearned is evil, the beauty of good women is evil if they stand without shame, and lineage is evil when its principle is gone.
93.nuance: Only killing is evil without condition (எல்லா விடத்தும்); the other three are goods that turn evil when something is lost. A family's standing is made to depend on its கொள்கை, its held principle, not on birth.

items.claim: killing is evil everywhere
letting one's children grow up unlearned is evil
the beauty of good women is evil if they lose shame
lineage is evil when its principle is destroyed

norm.note: a period norm making women's beauty a fault when it is not held in by நாண்

94.reading: The verse defines ஆசாரம் as learning, the rule of wealth as having enjoyment joined with dharma, justice as showing favour to no one, and says the king who rules with discernment does not lack inner searching.
94.nuance: A run of definitions (X என்பது Y). Calling ஆசாரம் simply learning is a strong claim beside the ritual sense of the word in the Acharakkovai. The division of the last two lines is not certain: உண்ணாட்டம் இன்மையும் இல் may mean the discerning ruler never fails to look inward, or that he lacks no inner inquiry.

items.claim: right conduct is learning
command of wealth is having enjoyment joined with dharma
justice is showing favour to no one
the ruler who rules with discernment does not lack inner inquiry

95.reading: The drunkard knows the misery of toddy, the highest of birds knows the misery of thirst, the man of many wives knows the misery of want, and the thief knows the misery of concealment.
95.nuance: Each misery is known only from inside: the one who suffers it is the only witness. புள்ளினுள் ஓங்கல் is most likely the bird said to drink only rain; the verse does not name it.

items.claim: the misery of toddy is known by the drunkard
the misery of thirst is known by the highest among birds
the misery of want is known by the man with many wives
the misery of concealment is known by the thief

96.reading: Wounding words appear in the mouths of the graceless, deceitful words do not appear in the mouths of the learned even when they die, evil talebearing does not appear in the mouths of the worthy, and deceitful words appear in the mouths of the base.
96.nuance: Two pairs of mouths: graceless and base speak, learned and worthy do not. கரப்புச்சொல் is repeated, once withheld and once spoken, which makes the verse a mirror. சாயிறுந் is probably a corruption of சாயினும், 'even if they die'.

items.claim: scarring words appear in the mouths of the graceless
deceitful words do not appear in the mouths of the learned even if they die
evil talebearing does not appear in the mouths of the worthy
deceitful words appear in the mouths of the base

97.reading: Those without beauty have no standing before bejewelled women, the unlearned man has none if he enters a fit assembly, and even a learned man has none if he falls among the unlearned and foolish.
97.nuance: Three items, not four: the verse names three who lose standing (பாடிலர், பாடிலன், பாடிலனே), and splitting கல்லாதார் பேதையார் into two audiences would not be defensible. The turn is the third: learning, which saves the second case, does not save one in the wrong audience.

items.claim: those without beauty have no standing before adorned women
the unlearned man has no standing in a fit assembly
even a learned man has no standing before the unlearned and foolish

98.reading: A gem does not lose its worth though it is soiled, dirt sticks to iron though it is smeared and polished, and the base, though bound and scoured, show their own dirt.
98.nuance: Three items: gem, iron and the base. The washing is the point: the gem needs none, the iron does not hold it, and the base, even scrubbed while held fast (பாசத்துள் இட்டு), show their nature again.

items.claim: a gem does not lose its worth though soiled
dirt clings to iron though it is coated
the base, though bound and polished, show their own dirt

99.reading: Not parting from the worthy one keeps company with is like the eye, living with those who do not care for one is like a wound, the rebuke of friends is like the lute, and a house without a woman of good character is like a ruin.
99.nuance: Four likenesses in ஒக்கும். The first word எண்ணொக்கும் is doubtful: as written it could mean 'like sesame' or 'like reckoning', and a reading 'like the eye' assumes கண். A friend's rebuke heard as lute music is the turn of the verse.

items.claim: not leaving the worthy one is close to is like the eye, if the doubtful first word is read so
living with those who do not care for one is like a wound
the rebuking words of friends are like the lute
a house without a woman of good nature is like a ruin

100.reading: If the tank is small the water overflows, if the household's income is small the wife takes over, if earlier penance was small deeds overrun one, and if strength is small the enemy overruns.
100.nuance: ஊரும் carries the verse: water spills over, and the others ride over the one who is too small to hold them. பெண்ணூரும் most likely means the wife overrides the husband when he brings in too little; it is a claim about the household, not a rule. மேலைத் தவம் is penance done before, perhaps in earlier lives.

items.claim: when a tank is small its water overflows
when the household's income is small the wife takes over
when earlier penance was small, karma overruns
when strength is small, enmity overruns

101.reading: Reviling yields reproach, doing obeisance yields thriving kin, wealth one has made yields enjoyment, and grace that has softened yields dharma.
101.nuance: A four-step table of causes, each with ஆகும். Enjoyment is tied to wealth and dharma to grace, not to wealth: the verse keeps the two apart.

items.claim: reviling yields reproach
doing obeisance yields thriving kin
wealth one has made yields enjoyment
softened grace yields dharma

102.reading: There is no one who knows everything, no one who knows nothing at all, no one whose faults hide every virtue, and no one who has learned all the arts.
102.nuance: The single closing இல் negates all four, so the verse is four 'there is none'. It denies both extremes of knowledge and both extremes of character at once. கணன் (the full count of the arts or treatises) is a rare word.

items.claim: there is no one who knows everything
there is no one who knows nothing at all
there is no one whose faults cover all his virtues
there is no one who has learned the whole range of learning

103.reading: The light of a house is its wife, the light of wives is worthy sons, the light of beloved sons is learning, and the light of learning is understanding that brings fame.
103.nuance: A chain: each light is lit by the next, so the house finally shines by understanding. The wife is the first link but not the last.

items.claim: the wife is the light of the house
worthy sons are the light of wives
learning is the light of beloved sons
understanding full of fame is the light of learning

104.reading: Sweet speech makes close kinship, harsh speech without sweetness makes a reviling mind, a tongue of gentle speech makes a mind of grace, and with that mind one reaches the release that does not perish.
104.nuance: A chain from the tongue to release: speech shapes the mind, and the mind gains வீடு. Harsh speech yields a fault in the speaker's own mind (வசைமனம்), not only others' anger. The verse is nearly the same as Sirupanchamoolam 89.

items.claim: sweet speech makes close kinship
harsh speech makes a reviling mind
a tongue of gentle speech makes a mind of grace
the one with that mind gains unperishing release

links.note: Thirikadugam joins people of a long line without learning to poverty; Nanmanikkadigai says lineage and family standing die beneath want of learning.
links.teaches: Thirikadugam names the outcome, poverty, and Nanmanikkadigai the death of the family's standing itself, so together they make unlearning ruin both the purse and the name of an old house.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu calls beauty in those without means painful; Nanmanikkadigai says beauty and youth die beneath poverty.
links.teaches: The two books say the same thing from two sides: Innaa names the sight of beauty in want painful, Nanmanikkadigai says the beauty itself does not survive it.

links.note: Kural 409 ranks the learned low-born above the unlearned high-born; Nanmanikkadigai says lineage dies beneath want of learning.
links.teaches: Where the Kural keeps high birth as a rank that learning outweighs, the quatrain makes the rank itself die without learning, a stronger claim about birth.
links.list_adds: It puts lineage in a row with beauty, paddy and a draught ox, so birth becomes one more thing that needs a support beneath it to live.

links.note: Kural 397 says every land and town becomes one's own, and asks why one stays unlearned; Nanmanikkadigai gives the belonging to the good and the renouncer, and ends with the man of wealth.
links.teaches: The Kural ties belonging everywhere to learning alone; the quatrain shows virtue, renunciation and plain wealth also open every town, and names the base for whom none opens.
links.list_adds: It splits the Kural's single case into four holders, three by virtue or vice and the last by money, and the last item ironically undoes the first.

links.note: Purananuru 192 opens with every town as ours and everyone our kin, as the stance of one who sees through the wise; Nanmanikkadigai says every town belongs to those with something in hand.
links.teaches: The heroic poem makes belonging everywhere a philosophical stance; the ethics verse observes that wealth secures the same welcome, which sets the ideal against how towns in fact receive people.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam counts the spider's eggs, the crab's young and abuse to the tongue as each one's own death; Nanmanikkadigai has the plantain's fruit and the unlearned man's own words.
links.teaches: Both books use a creature killed by its own offspring to say that speech kills the speaker, so the image of self-born death is a shared stock of the ethics group, applied each time to the tongue.

links.note: Kural 77 says dharma burns the loveless as the sun burns the boneless; Nanmanikkadigai calls dharma death to those who do wrong.
links.teaches: Read beside the plantain killed by its own fruit, the quatrain makes dharma a death the wrongdoer grows himself, which the Kural's sun, an outside force, does not show.
links.list_adds: It sets dharma's punishment among deaths that come from within the victim, so retribution becomes self-made rather than imposed.

links.note: Purananuru 187 says a land is good only where its men are good; Nanmanikkadigai says kings gain glory by the land they rule.
links.teaches: The pair runs the credit in opposite directions: the Purananuru makes the land's worth depend on its people, the ethics verse makes the king's glory depend on the land, so his glory rests on men he does not make good himself.

links.note: Kural 523 says life without mingling with kin is a tank with no bank; Nanmanikkadigai calls leaving one's kin striving after ruin.
links.teaches: The Kural shows the loss as waste, wealth spilling away; the quatrain names leaving kin as an effort, so ruin is something one works at rather than suffers.
links.list_adds: It sets abandoning kin as the one wrong striving after three right ones, so the last item reverses the verse's praise of effort.

links.note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, kind to every creature; Nanmanikkadigai names striving always after good as the mind of the அந்தணர்.
links.teaches: The Kural derives the name from the conduct; the quatrain lists the அந்தணர் with women and kings as a station with its proper striving, so read together they show the word moving between a status and a virtue.
links.list_adds: It puts the அந்தணர் in a row of stations, each with its own work, which turns the Kural's definition into a duty of a group.

links.note: Kural 284 says a love ripened in stealth yields undying sorrow; Nanmanikkadigai says not to steal because harsh things follow.
links.teaches: Both give the reason against theft as its consequence rather than its wrong, so the ethics books argue the point by outcome, not by rule.
links.list_adds: It sets theft beside rejecting the worthy, befriending the small and making enemies, so theft becomes one of four ways of making trouble for oneself.

links.note: Kural 871 says enmity should not be wanted even in jest; Nanmanikkadigai says one must not take up enmity with anyone.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the ban on enmity is absolute in both books: the Kural closes the gap of jest, the quatrain the gap of the opponent, with anyone at all.
links.list_adds: It sets avoiding enmity next to avoiding friendship with the small, so both who one befriends and who one opposes are guarded.

links.note: Kural 302 calls anger bad where it cannot avail and worse where it can; Nanmanikkadigai bids anger be curbed where it cannot avail.
links.teaches: The quatrain stops where the Kural's first half stops and, after bidding pride against enemies, leaves anger where one is strong unmentioned; the Kural's second half closes that gap.
links.list_adds: It sets curbing anger beside a call to be proud against enemies at the right time, so the anger left out is partly licensed by the list.

links.note: Kural 787 says friendship turns one from ruin and sets one on the path; Nanmanikkadigai says to increase friends by leading them to the good.
links.teaches: The Kural describes what a friend does; the quatrain turns that guidance into the way friendships multiply, so guiding friends is also how one gains more of them.
links.list_adds: It makes leading friends to the good a means of increase, set against diminishing food and anger, which turns a duty into a gain.

links.note: Kural 605 calls delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep the pleasure-boat of those bound for ruin; Nanmanikkadigai says sloth stays with those who are to perish.
links.teaches: The two books use the same phrase for the ruined (கெடுநீரார், கெடுவார்); the quatrain sets sloth's dwelling beside a tethered elephant, so sloth is pictured as a thing that stays, not a boat that carries one off.
links.list_adds: It puts sloth in a row with cruelty, women's shame and a tethered elephant under one verb, staying, so vice and restraint both become things that hold a person.

links.note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself; Nanmanikkadigai says bowing is always the ornament of the worthy.
links.teaches: The Kural plays bowing against self-adornment; the quatrain makes bowing itself the ornament, and sets it beside the Veda and victory, so humility is the learning proper to the worthy.
links.list_adds: It ranks humility among the proper excellences of each station, the andhanar's Veda and the king's just victory, making it the worthy man's own accomplishment.

links.note: Kural 57 asks what use confinement is and says a woman's own steadfastness is the best guard; Nanmanikkadigai says a woman without a bond goes as she pleases though guarded.
links.teaches: The Kural moves the guard inside the woman; the quatrain adds desire that flows on though blocked and murder that clings though hidden, so the failure of guarding becomes a general law about inner nature.
links.list_adds: It sets the guarded woman beside desire and a hidden killing, so the claim widens from women to everything that outward control cannot hold.

links.note: Kural 1253 has a woman say her desire breaks out like a sneeze though she would hide it; Nanmanikkadigai says desire goes where it was going though obstructed.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the experience in a lover's voice; the quatrain states it as a law beside a hidden killing, which shows the ethics books treating akam's confession as a fact about desire in general.
links.list_adds: It turns a lover's admission into one of four laws of what cannot be stopped or hidden, placed next to murder.

links.note: Kural 575 calls kindly regard the eye's only jewel and an eye without it a wound; Nanmanikkadigai says where the gentle eye of the worthy grows dharma grows.
links.teaches: The Kural judges the eye by its kindness; the quatrain gives each kind of eye its harvest, and makes the hard eye a source of strength in one line and of sin in another.
links.list_adds: It sets the gentle eye among four eyes, two of them hard, so kindly regard is ranked against daring and cruelty rather than praised alone.

links.note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even when without means; Nanmanikkadigai calls liberality at a time without means a fault.
links.teaches: On the plain reading the two disagree about giving when poor: the Kural praises it as knowledge of duty, the quatrain counts it a fault of timing, so the ethics books split over whether means limit generosity.
links.list_adds: It sets giving beyond one's means among faults of wrong timing, learning missed in youth and anger without kin, so liberality is judged by its season.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu calls the liberality of those without means painful; Nanmanikkadigai calls it a fault.
links.teaches: The two words differ: painful to see in Innaa, a fault in Nanmanikkadigai, so the same act is judged both by its cost to the giver and by its wrongness, and both books stand against the Kural 218 view.

links.note: Kural 306 says anger burns the raft of one's own kin; Nanmanikkadigai calls anger when one has no kin a fault.
links.teaches: Together they make kin and anger work both ways: anger destroys kin, and without kin anger has nothing to stand on, so the angry man loses the very support his anger needs.
links.list_adds: It counts anger without kin as a fault of wrong circumstance, beside youth without learning and giving without means.

links.note: Kural 67 says a father's good to his son is to place him in front in the assembly; Nanmanikkadigai calls letting children grow unlearned an evil.
links.teaches: The Kural states the father's duty as a gift; the quatrain states its neglect as an evil placed beside killing, which raises the weight of the duty.
links.list_adds: It ranks neglecting a child's learning with killing everywhere, so a parent's omission joins the gravest wrong in the list.

links.note: Kural 133 says conduct is noble birth and failing in it becomes low birth; Nanmanikkadigai says lineage is evil when its principle is destroyed.
links.teaches: The quatrain goes past the Kural's demotion to call the lost lineage itself an evil, and its கொள்கை, a held principle, names something narrower than conduct in general.
links.list_adds: It sets fallen lineage beside killing, unlearned children and shameless beauty, so birth is one more good turned evil by a loss.

links.note: Kural 541 says justice is investigating, showing favour to no one and acting after consideration; Nanmanikkadigai defines justice as having no favour toward anyone.
links.teaches: The same phrase (யார்மாட்டும் / யார்கண்ணும், no favour) defines justice in both, and the quatrain adds inner inquiry for the discerning ruler where the Kural asks for investigation, so the ruler's scrutiny is turned on himself as well.
links.list_adds: It sets the definition of justice beside definitions of conduct as learning and of wealth as enjoyment with dharma, making justice one of the ruler's set of defined virtues.

links.note: Acharakkovai 1 names learning as one of eight seeds of ஆசாரம்; Nanmanikkadigai says ஆசாரம் is learning.
links.teaches: The book of ஆசாரம் makes learning one root among eight and goes on to ritual rule, while the quatrain makes learning the whole of it, so the word is defined far more narrowly and less ritually here.

links.note: Kural 288 says deceit stands in the heart of those who know stealth; Nanmanikkadigai says the thief knows the misery of concealment.
links.teaches: The Kural shows deceit settled in the thief; the quatrain shows it as his torment, which only he knows, so the thief is both the home and the sufferer of his concealment.
links.list_adds: It sets the thief's misery among sufferings known only from inside, the drunkard's, the bird's and the many-wived man's.

links.note: Kural 139 says those with conduct cannot speak evil even by a slip; Nanmanikkadigai says deceitful words do not appear in the mouths of the learned even if they die.
links.teaches: The Kural rules out the accident, a slip; the quatrain rules out the extremity, death, so between them neither chance nor pressure draws evil speech from the good.
links.list_adds: It mirrors each good mouth with a bad one, the learned and worthy against the graceless and base, so the same kinds of word are shown present and absent.

links.note: Kural 720 likens holding forth before those not of one's kind to nectar spilled in a gutter; Nanmanikkadigai says even a learned man has no standing before the unlearned and foolish.
links.teaches: The Kural measures the waste of the speech; the quatrain measures the loss to the speaker, and pairs it with the unlearned man's loss before the fit assembly, so standing is shown to depend on the match of speaker and hearers.
links.list_adds: It makes the learned man's failure the mirror of the unlearned man's, so the list shows a mismatch failing in both directions.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 14 says fine points of learning spoken before the unlearned turn bad; Nanmanikkadigai says a learned man before the unlearned has no standing.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi says the words go bad, Nanmanikkadigai that the man loses standing, so the group counts the damage to both the teaching and the teacher.

links.note: Naladiyar 347 says a sandal of gold and gems is still for the foot, so the base are known by their deeds though wealthy; Nanmanikkadigai says the base, though bound and polished, show their dirt.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's base are dressed up by wealth, the quatrain's are scrubbed by force, and both fail, so neither fortune nor correction changes their nature.
links.list_adds: It sets the base against a gem that stays itself though soiled, so the base become the reverse of the gem, keeping their dirt as it keeps its worth.

links.note: Kural 784 says friendship is for going ahead to rebuke when one oversteps; Nanmanikkadigai likens friends' rebuking words to the lute.
links.teaches: The Kural states rebuke as the purpose of friendship; the quatrain says how it should be heard, as music, so the duty of the friend is matched by the response of the one rebuked.
links.list_adds: It sets the friend's rebuke among likenesses of company good and bad, so rebuke is counted as one of the pleasures of good company.

links.note: Verse 99 likens a house without a good woman to a ruin; verse 103 calls the wife the light of the house.
links.teaches: The book says the same thing from both sides, ruin without her and light with her, and 103 continues the chain to sons, learning and understanding, so her worth is the first link, not the whole.

links.note: Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which arrives first whatever one devises; Nanmanikkadigai says deeds overrun one when earlier penance was small.
links.teaches: The quatrain makes fate's power depend on how much penance was stored before, which limits the Kural's unqualified claim for fate.
links.list_adds: It sets karma's overrunning beside water spilling from a small tank and enemies overrunning the weak, so fate becomes one more force that breaks a container too small for it.

links.note: Kural 754 says rightly gained wealth yields both dharma and pleasure; Nanmanikkadigai gives pleasure to wealth and dharma to softened grace.
links.teaches: Where the Kural lets good wealth bear dharma, the quatrain assigns dharma to grace alone, which separates the two that the couplet joins.
links.list_adds: It lays out a table of causes in which wealth and grace sit side by side with different fruits, so dharma is pointedly not among wealth's results.

links.note: Verse 101 says reviling yields reproach; verse 104 says harsh speech yields a reviling mind.
links.teaches: Read together, the book places the reproach first in others' mouths and then in the speaker's own mind, so harsh speech damages the speaker twice.

links.note: Kural 503 says even the learned and flawless are rarely without blankness when examined; Nanmanikkadigai says no one knows everything and no one knows nothing.
links.teaches: The Kural speaks of the best; the quatrain adds the worst, so knowledge is never total and ignorance never total, which leaves everyone open to examination.
links.list_adds: It pairs no one all-knowing with no one all-ignorant, and the same for virtue and fault, so the list denies both extremes.

links.note: Kural 504 bids one weigh virtues and faults and take what predominates; Nanmanikkadigai says no one has faults that hide all virtue.
links.teaches: The quatrain supplies the ground for the Kural's method: since no one is pure fault, there are always virtues to weigh against the faults.
links.list_adds: It makes the mixed nature of people a general law beside the limits of knowledge, which is what the Kural's weighing needs.

links.note: Kural 60 calls a home's excellence its blessing and good children its ornament; Nanmanikkadigai makes the wife the light of the house, sons hers, learning theirs and understanding learning's.
links.teaches: The Kural stops at children; the quatrain continues the chain to learning and understanding, so the household's worth is finally measured by knowledge.
links.list_adds: It turns the couplet's pair into a chain of four lights, each lit by the next.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 89 has nearly the same lines: sweet speech makes kin, harsh speech enmity, gentle speech grace, and grace release.
links.teaches: The one variant matters: Sirupanchamoolam has harsh speech make enmity (பகைமை), Nanmanikkadigai a reviling mind (வசைமனம்), which moves the damage from one's relations to one's own mind.

links.note: Kural 96 says sweet speech of good things makes dharma grow; Nanmanikkadigai traces gentle speech through a mind of grace to release.
links.teaches: The Kural carries sweet speech to dharma in this life; the quatrain carries it through grace to வீடு, so speech becomes the first step of release.
links.list_adds: It makes speech the start of a chain ending in release, with harsh speech as the branch that turns the mind to blame.

source_issues: 96 line 2: சாயிறுந் is probably a corruption of சாயினும் ('even if they die').
99 line 1: எண்ணொக்கும் is doubtful; the sense 'like the eye' would need கண்ணொக்கும்.
104 is nearly the same verse as sirupanchamoolam:89 (variants கிழமை/கிளமை, வசைமனம்/பகைமை, அருள்மனம்/ஆரருள்); one book has likely taken it from the other or both from a common stock.
89 line 4 (அணங்கல் வணங்கின்று பெண்) is obscure as written.
